stimulus.title: Drill D1 · Psicologia · alvo: 4 min
stimulus.content:
Narrator: Listen to part of a talk in a psychology class.

Professor: We've been discussing decision-making, and today I want to bring up something researchers call the paradox of choice. The idea is counterintuitive: you'd think more options would always make us happier, but past a certain point it does the opposite.

A classic example. In one well-known study, researchers set up a tasting table in a grocery store: first with six varieties of jam, then with twenty-four. You'd expect the bigger display to sell more. Actually, the smaller display generated significantly more purchases. The larger one attracted more browsers, but far fewer of them bought anything.

Why? Two things: decision fatigue and anticipated regret. With more options, comparing them mentally becomes exhausting — that's the fatigue. And even before you pick, you start worrying that one of the other twenty-three might be better and that you'll regret your choice — that's the regret. Ironically, more choices can leave people feeling back to square one, unable to commit at all.

Now, this doesn't mean choice is bad: a complete absence of options is its own problem. The point is there's a sweet spot, and past it, additional options stop helping and start working against us. To be fair, later studies haven't always replicated the jam result, so the size of the effect is still debated.

prompt: Gist-content. What is the talk mainly about?

options.A: Grocery stores should minimize the products they display
options.B: Beyond a point, more options can reduce satisfaction and hinder decisions
options.C: Consumers always prefer smaller displays
options.D: Decision fatigue affects only in-store shoppers

explanation: Tese anunciada no início e no fechamento. (A) exagera; (C) "always" nunca é dito; (D) está fora do que foi dito.

stimulus.title: Drill D2 · Biologia · alvo: 4 min
stimulus.content:
Narrator: Listen to part of a talk in a biology class.

Professor: When we picture a forest, we tend to see individual trees competing — for light, for water, for space. And that's real. But over the last thirty years, research has revealed something the old picture missed: the trees are also connected, underground, through fungi.

Here's how. The roots of most trees are wrapped in a network of fungal threads; this partnership between root and fungus is called a mycorrhiza. The fungi pull in water and minerals the tree's roots can't reach efficiently, and hand them to the tree. In return, the tree gives the fungi sugars it makes through photosynthesis. So far, a simple trade.

The surprising part is that a single fungal network can link many trees at once — even trees of different species. And things move along those links. Experiments using radioactive tracers have shown carbon flowing from a tree standing in full sun to a shaded seedling of another species nearby. Some researchers describe old, well-connected trees as "hub trees" that support younger ones around them.

Now, a word of caution. This work has captured the public imagination, and some popular accounts overstate it: talking about forests as single cooperative organisms. The jury's still out on how deliberate or widespread the sharing really is. What's solid is that the connections exist and that resources can move through them. How much that reshapes our model of the forest is still being worked out.

prompt: Gist-content. What is the main point of the talk?

options.A: Trees in a forest only compete, never cooperate
options.B: Trees are connected underground through fungal networks, and resources can move between them
options.C: Mycorrhizal fungi are harmful to most trees
options.D: Forests are single cooperative organisms

explanation: O professor admite a competição mas acrescenta a conexão. (A) ignora a segunda metade da tese; (C) é o oposto (a relação é benéfica); (D) é exatamente o exagero que ele critica no fim.

stimulus.title: Drill D3 · História da tecnologia · alvo: 4 min
stimulus.content:
Narrator: Listen to part of a talk in a history of technology class.

Professor: Look at your keyboard. The top row of letters spells Q-W-E-R-T-Y. It's an odd arrangement — the most common letters aren't under your strongest fingers. So why has it survived, essentially unchanged, for a hundred and fifty years?

The layout dates from the 1870s, from early mechanical typewriters. The common story is that QWERTY was designed to slow typists down so the metal type-bars wouldn't jam. That's probably an oversimplification (the real design pressures were more mixed), but the key point is that the layout was shaped by the constraints of 1870s machinery, constraints that vanished decades ago.

Better layouts have been proposed. The best known, Dvorak, was patented in 1936 and, in some studies, allows modestly faster and more comfortable typing. Yet it never caught on. Why not?

This is a textbook case of what economists call path dependence, or sometimes "lock-in." Once QWERTY became the standard, everything organized itself around that standard: typewriters were built for it, typing was taught on it, and every new typist learned it because that's what the machines used — and machines used it because that's what typists knew. To switch, a single person gains little unless nearly everyone switches at once. The cost of coordinating that switch is enormous, and no one bears it. So an arrangement that made sense only for 1870s hardware is still, quietly, on every device you own.

prompt: Gist-content. What is the talk mainly about?

options.A: How to type faster using the Dvorak layout
options.B: Why an outdated keyboard layout has persisted, as an example of path dependence
options.C: The mechanical design of 19th-century typewriters
options.D: Why Dvorak is objectively the best possible layout

explanation: A pergunta central é por que um layout ultrapassado sobreviveu, e a resposta é path dependence. (A)/(D) mudam o foco/exageram; (C) é contexto, não o tema.

stimulus.content: **TRANSCRIÇÃO (trecho de palestra · Introdução à Sociologia):** "Today we're discussing the concept of social capital · the networks of relationships and mutual trust that allow individuals and communities to function effectively. Unlike financial capital, social capital isn't stored in a bank account; it exists in the quality and density of a person's relationships. Researchers distinguish between two types: bonding social capital, which strengthens ties within a tightly knit group (like an extended family or a close friend circle) and bridging social capital, which connects individuals across different groups, such as different professions or social classes. Communities strong in bonding capital but weak in bridging capital often show high internal solidarity but limited access to outside resources and opportunities."

stimulus.content: **TRANSCRIÇÃO (trecho · Introdução à Biologia):** "So far we've treated the cell membrane as a simple barrier, but that picture is misleading. The membrane is better thought of as a busy checkpoint. It's selectively permeable · some molecules, like oxygen and water, pass through freely; others, like glucose or charged ions, can only cross with help, through specific protein channels or pumps. And here's the key point for today: some of those pumps run *against* the concentration gradient. They move a substance from where it's scarce to where it's already abundant, which costs energy. This is called active transport, and it's how a nerve cell, for example, maintains the sharp difference in ion concentration across its membrane that makes a nerve impulse possible."

stimulus.title: Listen to an Academic Talk
stimulus.content: **TRANSCRIÇÃO:** "Let's turn to a phenomenon economists call 'loss aversion' · the tendency for people to feel the pain of a loss more intensely than the pleasure of an equivalent gain. Classic experiments show that people typically demand roughly twice as much to give something up as they were willing to pay to acquire it in the first place · a pattern known as the endowment effect. This has real consequences outside the lab. Investors, for instance, often hold onto losing stocks far longer than rational analysis would justify, simply because selling would mean formally realizing the loss. The discomfort of that realization outweighs, for many people, the objective financial logic of cutting their losses early."
